about.title: Dinuba Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Dinuba's economy leans heavily on agriculture, packing houses, and the trucking that moves goods along routes like Avenue 416 and El Monte Way — work that carries real physical risk. When someone is hurt on the job here, California generally routes the claim through workers' compensation, which pays regardless of fault but limits what you can recover from your employer directly. That's not always the end of the story, though. If a piece of faulty equipment, a subcontractor, or a negligent driver on a road like Alta Avenue contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside workers' comp. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect injured workers in Dinuba with an independent attorney who can look at the full picture, sort out which claims apply, and explain your options without cost or obligation to you.

items.title: Understanding Comp vs. Third-Party Claims
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like an equipment manufacturer or another driver — may still owe you a separate claim. An attorney can help sort out which path, or both, applies to your situation.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation
items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting a workplace injury. If you've faced pushback after reporting within the required 30-day window, an attorney can address that separately from your injury claim.

items.title: Watching the Clock on Deadlines
items.desc: Reporting an injury to your employer has a strict 30-day window, and any third-party injury claim generally carries a two-year deadline. Missing either can close doors, so getting matched with an attorney early matters.

items.question: I work at a packing house near Alta Avenue — can I still file a claim if the accident was partly my fault?
items.answer: Workers' compensation in California generally doesn't require proving fault, so it typically covers you regardless of how the incident happened. If a third party, like equipment maker or delivery driver, also contributed to the injury, a separate fault-based claim might be possible too. An independent attorney can review the specifics and explain what applies to your case.

items.question: My employer said I have no case since I got hurt driving for work near El Monte Way. Is that true?
items.answer: Not necessarily. If another driver caused or contributed to the crash, you may have a third-party injury claim in addition to any workers' comp coverage. That third-party claim generally carries its own two-year filing deadline, so it's worth having it reviewed promptly.

items.question: What if I reported my injury late because I wasn't sure how serious it was?
items.answer: California generally expects injuries to be reported to your employer within 30 days, so delays can complicate a claim. It doesn't automatically mean you're out of options, though — an attorney can look at the timeline and any documentation to see what can still be done.
